title: The Red Army Strikes Back
subtitle: Soviet counteroffensives and the limits of German momentum
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: Soviet counteroffensives, relief attempts, Mogilev’s resistance and the developing Yelnya salient.
body:
On 19 July 1941, the Soviet General Staff instructed reserve armies to concentrate for an operation intended to encircle German forces around Smolensk. Its instructions followed individual divisions through railway stations, road junctions, and assembly areas. Some were to travel by train, others on foot, and one with the help of trucks borrowed from another command. These practical details expose the distance between possessing reserves on an organisational chart and assembling a force capable of attacking. The proposed operation depended on several bodies of men arriving from different directions, with their weapons and supplies, while the battle they were entering continued to change. [1] By 23 July, Soviet attacks were developing across a broad arc around Smolensk, directed against the flanks and communications of the German advance. Their common purpose concealed considerable differences in readiness. Some formations were still assembling, others had already been checked, and several headquarters lacked current information about the troops they were expected to coordinate. The chapter’s central problem is how an intended concentric offensive became a succession of engagements that German forces could confront separately. Its outcome affected the invader’s freedom of action while consuming reserves the Soviet command urgently needed for the defence that followed.

Reserves arriving in different ways

The [previous chapter](/articles/barbarossa-smolensk-under-assault-1941-07-16) followed the German entry into Smolensk and the continued fighting for the city and its approaches. By the third week of July, Soviet headquarters faced a wider problem. Armies west of the new German penetrations needed a connection with the east, while reserve formations approaching the battlefield required space in which to deploy. An attack from outside could relieve pressure on the threatened armies, disrupt German supply routes, and restore a more coherent front. These were connected objectives, although achieving the first did not guarantee the others. [2] The geography offered several approaches. North of Smolensk, forces assembling around Bely could advance southwest toward Dukhovshchina, a town behind the German positions near Yartsevo. Farther south, troops around Roslavl could move northwest along the road toward Pochinok and Smolensk. Between them, formations near the Vop River and Yartsevo could strike westward. If these advances converged, German units projecting east of Smolensk might themselves become encircled. The plan attempted to turn the extended shape of the German advance into a vulnerability. It also demanded cooperation across a battlefield where Soviet communications were already unreliable. [3] The movement order of 19 July reveals how difficult that cooperation would be to arrange. The 29th Army was to bring the 252nd, 256th, and 243rd Rifle Divisions toward the Toropets sector. The 243rd was assigned railway unloading points; other formations were to march. The 30th Army was to concentrate the 242nd, 251st, and 250th Rifle Divisions farther south. Trucks were allocated to assist the 242nd, including vehicles from a transport battalion and the Reserve Front. These instructions show an attempt to accelerate a specific formation, rather than evidence that the reserve armies enjoyed general motor transport. [1] Near Roslavl, the force becoming Kachalov’s group faced a concentration problem of its own, with rifle divisions moving by road. Across the proposed offensive, different modes of transport produced unequal arrival times for infantry, artillery and supporting services. This made concentration a process whose completion had to be established through reports. Receiving the leading elements of a division could provide troops for immediate action while leaving the force without what it required for a sustained attack. Headquarters’ choices about when to commit those arrivals consequently shaped both the pressure imposed on the Germans and the cohesion of the Soviet operation.

The shape of the Soviet counteroffensive

General Staff instructions received on 21 July named groups under Maslennikov, Khomenko, Kalinin, and Kachalov. Rokossovsky’s improvised force already operated nearer Yartsevo. These names should not suggest five equally complete armies. They identified commands being assembled from available formations for particular tasks. Maslennikov’s troops covered the northern approaches around Toropets. Khomenko’s force was to attack toward Dukhovshchina; Kalinin’s formations were being brought toward the Vop sector; Kachalov would advance from the south. Their relationship evolved as units arrived and assignments changed. [4] Western Front Order 0076, issued on 21 July, translated this concentration into a more immediate plan. Khomenko was to move out of the forested and marshy assembly region and attack on 23 July toward Dukhovshchina. The 50th and 53rd Cavalry Divisions were assigned work against German rear areas and communications, as well as protection against threats from the Velizh direction. Cavalry offered mobility without requiring fuel for every mounted soldier, but still required passable routes, fodder, reconnaissance, and coordination. Its presence is a reminder that Soviet attempts to manoeuvre extended beyond the surviving tank formations. [3] Rokossovsky’s group received a complementary mission from the Vop sector. The order listed the 101st and 107th Tank Divisions, rifle formations, and an antitank regiment among the forces intended for this operation. Their first objective was cooperation against the German grouping near Dukhovshchina; a subsequent movement toward Smolensk was envisaged. Meanwhile, Kachalov’s 145th and 149th Rifle Divisions and 104th Tank Division were to advance along the Smolensk road from the Roslavl area. The successive orders did not always list identical tank formations, another reason to read each document with its date rather than combine them into a timeless order of battle. [3] [4] The missions given to armies already in action were intended to connect the new attacks to the existing battle. The 20th Army was to disrupt the German rear, the 22nd to hold enemy forces in place, and the 13th to act towards Propoisk and Krichev, with aviation supporting the attacking groups. The conception depended on these effects reinforcing one another. If one army held German troops while another threatened their communications, the enemy’s ability to concentrate against either would diminish. Uneven timing weakened precisely that relationship, allowing separate German responses to pressures intended to be simultaneous.[3]

What the reports actually showed

The Western Front’s situation report for the evening of 23 July provides a sobering comparison with the orders. Kalinin’s formations were still concentrating. The 91st Rifle Division had reached its assembly area by midnight on 22 July; the report placed the 89th elsewhere and had no information on the 166th. No current report had arrived from Khomenko’s group, and steps were being taken to restore communications. The published collection’s editorial note preserves an earlier report showing leading elements ahead of the main bodies and cavalry still completing its movement from unloading points. [5] Rokossovsky’s sector was equally unsettled. The report described his troops regrouping on the eastern bank of the Vop after fighting along the river. The 107th Tank Division had reached a named concentration area, but information on the 101st was missing. The 38th Rifle Division had withdrawn under repeated air attacks and artillery and mortar fire, destroying crossings behind it. That last action makes the operational difficulty especially clear. A force preparing to attack westward had been compelled to secure an eastern-bank defensive position and deny bridges to the enemy. Reversing that movement would require another crossing effort. [5] Kachalov’s group made measurable progress from the south. At 17:00 on 23 July, headquarters reported that it had driven back German forward elements and was fighting at crossings of the Stomet River, approximately eighteen kilometres southeast of Pochinok. German aircraft were attacking continuously, according to the report. This places the force on its intended approach, but still short of the junctions needed for a decisive convergence. On 24 July, the Western Direction command reported that Kachalov was fighting for a second day south of Pochinok. Movement had begun; the timetable envisioned in the attack order had not been fulfilled. [5] [6] The 24 July report placed the opening of attacks by Khomenko, Kalinin and the 107th Tank Division that morning. It also described heavy German air activity and movements interpreted as preparations for a counterstroke. Set beside the previous evening’s summary, it shows how the planned convergence unfolded through staggered commitments. The interval gave German commanders scope to confront successive threats and disturbed Soviet expectations about support from neighbouring groups. This chronological distinction is necessary to explain the operation’s limited effect: the force available across the whole scheme was never equivalent to the force acting together at a particular point and hour. [6]

Ammunition, wounded men, and the limits of command

The northern sector illustrates why reinforcements could not simply be directed at the most promising point on a map. The 22nd Army was establishing a defensive line along the Lovat while helping formations escape encirclement nearer Nevel. Its 179th Rifle Division defended Velikiye Luki and used part of its force in an attack toward Nevel. The 62nd Rifle Corps was attempting to bring out remnants of the 134th Rifle Division discovered north of Velizh. These simultaneous responsibilities absorbed troops that might otherwise have contributed to a larger offensive. For a commander on this flank, saving an isolated formation, defending a town, and preparing an attack were competing demands within the same day. [5] The 170th Rifle Division’s southwestward attack to assist the encircled 51st Corps had an unconfirmed result at 18:00. This uncertainty gave the relief effort an immediate human dimension. Wounded soldiers in the pocket could not exploit an opportunity to escape as readily as mobile troops, while those sent to open a route had to fight with the resources available nearby. The urgency of evacuation increased the pressure to attack without solving the shortages that restricted success. The relationship between relief and medical transport therefore belongs within the operational explanation: it shaped the purposes for which scarce fighting strength was committed. [5] The counteroffensive’s logistical problems reached beyond fuel for tanks. Headquarters had to find formations, establish telephone or radio contact, move ammunition to guns, and arrange medical evacuation while routes changed hands. The 23 July summary recorded up to two thousand wounded people remaining unevacuated in the medical establishments of the encircled 51st Rifle Corps farther north. The same report described efforts by neighbouring formations to help troops escape. The evacuation problem belonged directly to the operational situation: holding or opening a route could determine whether wounded soldiers could be moved at all. [5] Elsewhere, the meaning of a division’s name had become equally precarious. Near Smolensk, the report described the trained and armed elements of the 127th and 158th Rifle Divisions available for a particular attack as roughly six hundred and one hundred men respectively, with almost no machine guns. These are figures for the specified forces in that report, not reliable totals for every person belonging to the divisions. Their attack against the railway junction at Ryabtsevo failed. The account’s detailed hours are internally awkward, but its broader conclusion is clear: depleted troops were being committed against an enemy possessing artillery, armour, and motorised infantry. [5] Soviet command understood that firepower could alter such encounters, but ammunition availability constrained its use. On 24 July, Timoshenko and Shaposhnikov reported successful rocket fire against German troops near Rudnya and requested additional batteries with ammunition. Their report credited three salvos with substantial effects and stated that only three salvos remained. The claimed German losses cannot be accepted without corroboration. The ammunition statement nevertheless exposes a practical limitation: a weapon’s impressive first employment did not establish a sustainable supply of fire. A battery could influence a local battle and still lack the ammunition required for the next one. [6]

Firepower and replenishment

Three salvos remaining

In their report of 24 July, Timoshenko and Shaposhnikov praised the effect of three rocket salvos against German troops near Rudnya, then stated that the battery had ammunition for only three more. They requested additional batteries and charges. The reported enemy losses remain uncorroborated; the ammunition statement is a specific claim about the means available for further action. The document also had a persuasive purpose, using the weapon’s asserted success to support a request for resources. Read with that qualification, it explains why a powerful local concentration of fire did not establish a sustainable capacity to repeat the result.

[6]

German gains and German obligations

Another improvised reinforcement reached the records on 24 July: a motorised regiment formed from men of the withdrawn 17th Mechanised Corps. Headquarters reported sending it from Yartsevo to Lukin at 16:00 on the previous day, describing its infantry strength as sixteen hundred bayonets. The terminology indicates the fighting category being reported, rather than a complete accounting of everyone attached to the unit. It also shows how the Soviet command attempted to recover military value from formations damaged in earlier battles. Survivors were reorganised and returned to action under a new arrangement. That process could preserve experienced men, but it could not instantly recreate their former corps’ equipment, supporting services, or established command relationships. [6] The Soviet attacks confronted German formations whose success had carried them into an increasingly complicated position. Mobile units had moved beyond infantry support, while surviving Soviet forces occupied pockets and threatened the routes between them. The Germans needed to destroy those forces, maintain their own communications, and prepare further operations. Each task competed for troops and time. The Soviet counteroffensive did not recover the freedom of movement its planners wanted, but it intensified the work required to secure the German advance. [7] German discussion in the following days confirms that this was an operational problem, not merely a later explanation for delay. During a visit to Army Group Centre on 25 July, Keitel conveyed Hitler’s preference for smaller encirclements with less separation between armour and infantry. As reconstructed in Blau’s U.S. Army study, the concern was that broad envelopments allowed substantial Soviet forces to escape and exposed valuable armour to attacks on its flanks. German air reconnaissance had observed columns leaving the Smolensk area through an eastern gap. Even after the spectacular advances of mid-July, the destruction of the encircled armies remained incomplete. [7] The debate over Germany’s next move developed from these existing commitments. Mobile formations remained engaged in containment, flank protection and renewed fighting while infantry and services attempted to close the distance behind them. Any proposal for a new advance or a transfer to another sector therefore required an account of how those tasks would be completed or reassigned. Command disagreement influenced strategy, but the disagreement concerned forces whose availability was already conditional. Evaluating a choice requires examining what it demanded from that military system and which risks it accepted, rather than treating an alternative direction as an operation that could begin without preparation. Glantz’s study of neglected Soviet operations distinguishes the coordination pursued by higher headquarters from the cooperation achieved by formations in battle. He argues that repeated assignments exceeded available capabilities and produced severe losses. The July documents supply a closely observed instance of that problem: converging objectives coexist with unfinished concentration, missing reports and resistance encountered before the scheduled junctions. Soviet initiative imposed further work on the invader while the way it was exercised consumed valuable capacity. The effects have to be assessed together to explain why continuing resistance could complicate German plans without delivering the recovery Soviet commanders envisaged. [8]

Mogilev and the people behind the positions

Southwest of the principal Smolensk fighting, Mogilev remained an important centre of resistance on the Dnieper. The 23 July summary described the 61st Rifle Corps under heavy attack and reported that German forces had taken Lupolovo on the previous day. It also recorded unsuccessful Soviet attacks toward Krichev and fighting near Propoisk. These actions belonged to an effort to contest the routes between the central battlefield and its southern flank. They also demonstrate that the counteroffensive was being attempted while other Soviet formations fought to avoid isolation or destruction. [5] The Western Direction’s report of 24 July called for an operation to connect with the encircled Mogilev corps. Its claims that the defenders had defeated German divisions should be treated as contemporary claims, not accepted casualty assessments. More concrete is the continuing requirement to relieve the position. The air force section of the previous evening’s summary recorded supplies being dropped at Mogilev’s airfield. Aerial delivery could assist an isolated force, but this report gives no tonnage and provides no basis for assuming that it met the corps’ needs. The attempt itself shows that ordinary ground supply had become insufficiently secure. [6] [5] Around Mogilev, the contraction of military routes also restricted civilian choices. Roads carrying troops towards a possible exit could be needed by households attempting to move east; workplaces might become evacuation priorities, remain sources of subsistence or fall into the hands of the occupier. Access to transport and information was unequal, so the movement of a formation cannot stand in for the experience of the population along its route. The later testimony discussed below enters at a different scale. It identifies an individual’s observation of occupation violence while leaving its precise date unresolved, preserving evidence without fitting it artificially to the operational calendar. The occupation following the battle brought forced labour and anti-Jewish murder. Yahad–In Unum preserves witness testimony and documentary evidence of that violence. This later evidence establishes dangers facing those who remained; it cannot assign every crime to 23 July. The civilian experience must retain its own chronology alongside the military one. [9]

A witness whose date remains uncertain

Natalia V., born in 1926, was interviewed in Mogilev by Yahad–In Unum in April 2012. She recalled seeing a covered truck while working in a field, then watching Jews forced out and shot beside a pit. The published excerpt identifies summer but supplies no exact date or year for the event. It therefore cannot document a shooting on 23 July 1941. Its value here is different: it preserves a civilian witness’s account of violence during the subsequent German occupation. Retaining that limit allows her testimony to enter the history without borrowing a precision it does not possess. The long interval before the interview also needs to remain visible to the reader. [9]

A coalition taking shape beyond the battlefield

The Soviet state’s continued resistance affected decisions well beyond Smolensk. Britain had already entered a wartime agreement with the Soviet Union, while the United States was considering assistance without being a belligerent against Germany. For Poland’s government in exile, cooperation with Moscow raised a separate problem: the state now fighting Germany had participated in Poland’s destruction in 1939. The diplomatic negotiations underway in July connected immediate military survival to unresolved questions of territory, prisoners, and sovereignty. The [Poland studies](/campaigns/poland-1939) explain that earlier rupture; here its importance lies in the difficulty of building a coalition after it. [10] An American memorandum of 8 July records the Polish ambassador asking Washington to encourage an agreement with the Soviet government. Sumner Welles agreed to express support in general terms but declined to enter into the details of negotiations already taking place in London. This was an identifiable limit to American involvement, rather than a settled programme for the Eastern Front. It also shows that Allied cooperation was being negotiated among governments with different interests and different leverage. The agreement eventually signed on 30 July belongs to the next chapter’s chronology. It should not be treated as an accomplished fact while the Soviet counteroffensive of 23 July was beginning. [10] Diplomatic expectations did not remove the immediate burdens borne by Soviet formations. The units near Bely, Yartsevo, and Roslavl still depended on supplies already available to them and on the Soviet transport system’s ability to deliver more. No pledge made abroad could instantly replace an artillery battery’s expended ammunition or evacuate wounded men from an encircled corps. Nevertheless, continued resistance preserved the possibility that a longer coalition war would develop. Its political consequence was therefore connected to its military endurance, even when a particular Soviet attack failed to reach its assigned objective.

The position reached

There was also a difference between reopening a supply route and restoring the earlier front. Timoshenko and Shaposhnikov’s report of 24 July expressed an ambition to destroy the German groupings north and south of Smolensk, straighten the front, and create supply routes for a rapid advance toward Vitebsk, Orsha, and Mogilev. The sequence joined a necessary local task to a much larger prospective recovery. The first depended on keeping battered armies supplied; the second assumed those armies could regain substantial offensive strength. Read beside the same report’s requests for ammunition and complaints about communications, the ambition reveals how far Soviet expectations still exceeded their immediate means. [6] The positions documented on 23 and 24 July reveal the operation’s uneven development. Kachalov’s southern group fought at river crossings, northern formations entered action at different times, troops inside Smolensk mounted local attacks, and formations elsewhere struggled to escape encirclement. A single westward arrow would conceal the relationships among these actions. For the atlas, the essential distinction is between an assigned direction and confirmed movement, including the intervals when headquarters could establish neither position nor result. For the historical argument, that uncertainty helps explain why the Soviet command could not combine its available strength into the decisive convergence it intended. By the evening of 23 July, the Red Army had demonstrated that German penetrations would encounter further organised opposition. It had not produced the coordinated encirclement envisaged in its orders. Reports from the following day show continued fighting, delayed attacks, German countermeasures, and uncertainty about events around Yelnya. In that sector, the Western Direction command complained that the relevant headquarters lacked reliable contact with their troops. A reported German withdrawal could not be confidently converted into an operational success when the command itself did not know how the fighting had ended. [6] The counteroffensive’s consequences extended beyond the ground recovered. Soviet attacks helped keep German formations engaged around positions whose earlier capture had appeared decisive, while depleted Soviet units lost further capacity in attempts that failed to converge. Both effects shaped the choices available at the end of July. German commanders had to secure and replenish their advancing forces; Soviet commanders had to rebuild a defence using reserves already expended in unsuccessful attacks. The [30 July chapter](/articles/barbarossa-a-strategy-under-strain-1941-07-30) examines how those material conditions entered the strategic debate, alongside the diplomatic efforts to sustain a longer war.

sourceMethod: Unpublished review draft. Numbered references link to the bibliography and return to their first use. Specific document, paragraph and page locators accompany the references. Soviet military records were read in Russian transcription from the published General Staff collections; English descriptions are paraphrases by the atlas, and archival identifiers are those printed in the collections, not claims of direct archival inspection. Orders establish intentions; situation reports contain contemporary information, estimates and gaps. U.S. Army retrospective studies are read critically alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Publisher excerpts are cited only for inspected passages. Testimony is distinguished from contemporary reporting. Dates in titles anchor the chronology; subsequent developments are dated explicitly. The atlas layers are qualified regional interpretations; their boundaries and arrows are not independent evidence of exact control or unit positions.
